## Week 10: evaluation, distribution shift and deployment

What a winning score shows, and what it does not. The leaderboard first: comparing two models on the same rows, paired; Hoeffding's inequality and the union bound, which say how far every score can be from its risk at once; choosing the comparison before the test rows are opened; the bootstrap for numbers that are not averages; and scores that drift when the candidates are tuned to them. Then the data move: in-distribution against out-of-distribution generalization, covariate shift and reweighting by a ratio of probabilities, label shift and a change of intercept, and what each shift does to accuracy, calibration and ranking. Last, scores and decisions: curve fitting with and without a theory behind it, what a competition win does and does not license, a cost score used to allocate extra care that is accurate and calibrated and still allocates it unequally, and prediction tasks that a better score would not make better. Data: synthetic patient-years from a study of a commercial health algorithm ([data note](data/obermeyer.html)).

**Reading [PROVISIONAL]**

- PPA, chapter 8 ("Datasets"), the sections "Longevity of benchmarks", "Harms associated with data" (its parts on privacy and on problem framing) and "Limits of data and prediction". Web version: [mlstory.org/data.html](https://mlstory.org/data.html).
- Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C. and Mullainathan, S. (2019), "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations", *Science* 366(6464), 447--453, [doi:10.1126/science.aax2342](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aax2342).

Optional: Rodu, J. and Baiocchi, M. (2023), "When black box algorithms are (not) appropriate: a principled prediction-problem ontology", *Observational Studies*, [arXiv:2001.07648](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07648), sections 1 and 2.
